rw: The FOMC is the Federal Reserve committee that votes on monetary policy, including the target range for the federal funds rate, so this option describes its real role accurately.

ww.A committee that sets the minimum wage a: Wage and hours rules come from labor law and the Department of Labor, not the FOMC, whose job is monetary policy and interest rate targets rather than employment rules.
ww.A committee that sets stock prices on th: Stock prices are set continuously by buyers and sellers in the market, not by a committee each morning, and the FOMC has no role in setting individual share prices.
ww.A committee that audits brokerages and r: Auditing brokerages and reporting to the SEC and FINRA is regulatory oversight work done by other bodies, while the FOMC focuses on interest rates and the money supply.

rw: Dark pools are private trading venues where orders are not shown to the public until after execution, which helps large investors trade big blocks without moving the market price.

ww.Trading by hackers who break into accoun: Dark pool trading is a legal, regulated activity run by brokers and exchanges, not something done by hackers breaking into accounts to place secret orders.
ww.Trading in a company's own shares by its: Employees trading their own company's shares has nothing to do with dark pools, and that kind of insider activity is governed by separate rules on insider trading and blackout periods.
ww.Trading that happens only at night while: Dark pools operate during normal market hours alongside public exchanges, so they are defined by hidden order visibility rather than by trading only at night when markets are closed.

rw: After-hours trading is any trading outside the regular exchange session of 9:30 a.m. to 4 p.m. Eastern, such as the evening extended session, which is exactly what this option states.

ww.Trading by employees after work in their: After-hours trading is defined by the time on the clock, not by who trades or why, so it is not limited to employees dealing in their own company's stock.
ww.Trading in bonds only with stocks not al: After-hours sessions allow stocks and many other securities to trade, so saying it covers only bonds while stocks are barred is false and misdescribes the extended sessions.
ww.Trading that occurs only on weekends and: After-hours trading happens on regular business days just after the close and before the open, so limiting it to weekends and holidays misses how extended sessions actually work.

rw: Fewer participants means lower volume, and thinner order books produce wider bid-ask spreads and bigger price swings, which makes after-hours fills more expensive and riskier than daytime trades.

ww.It is illegal for most investors: After-hours trading is legal and open to most investors through their brokers, so illegality is not the reason it is riskier, and this option states something that is simply false.
ww.The exchange adds a penalty fee: Exchanges do not add a penalty fee for extended-hours trades, and any broker charges are ordinary costs, so a penalty fee is not the main source of added risk.
ww.Prices are fixed until the open: Prices are not frozen until the open, since trades continue and quotes move after hours, often sharply on news, so fixed prices would remove risk instead of adding it.

rw: An earnings surprise is the gap between reported earnings and the consensus analyst estimate, and a positive or negative gap often moves the stock price sharply after the announcement.

ww.A bonus paid to employees when the firm: Employee bonuses for beating sales goals are internal pay decisions and do not define an earnings surprise, which compares reported profit with outside analyst forecasts instead.
ww.A change in the CEO that surprises inves: A CEO change can surprise investors, but it is a management event and not an earnings surprise, which refers only to results versus the analyst consensus.
ww.An unexpected dividend paid out to share: An unexpected dividend is a payout decision by the board, whereas an earnings surprise measures how far reported profit differs from what analysts had predicted for the quarter.

rw: A 10b5-1 plan lets insiders set up trades in advance on a preset schedule, which helps show the trades were not based on material nonpublic information at the time.

ww.A plan to split a stock into more shares: A stock split is a corporate action that raises the share count and lowers the price, and it has nothing to do with the scheduled insider trading described by Rule 10b5-1.
ww.A plan to merge two companies into one l: A merger of two companies is a corporate deal handled through other filings and approvals, and it is unrelated to the pre-arranged insider trading plan this rule creates.
ww.A plan to raise capital from bondholders: Raising capital by selling new bonds is a debt issuance carried out by the company with an underwriter, not the insider trading schedule governed by Rule 10b5-1.

rw: Regulation FD requires public companies to release material information to everyone at the same time, so no select analyst or large investor gets an unfair advantage over other holders.

ww.A rule that bans short selling in any st: Short selling bans after a one-day drop are different measures, such as the alternative uptick rule, and Regulation FD deals with disclosure of information instead of short sale limits.
ww.A rule that sets the commission on trade: Commission levels on brokerage trades are set by the brokers and competition, and Regulation FD does not regulate fees, only how companies release material information to investors.
ww.A rule setting the interest rate on loan: Mortgage interest rates are set by lenders and market conditions, and they have nothing to do with Regulation FD, which governs corporate disclosure to investors and analysts.

rw: Form 8-K is the current report public companies file with the SEC to disclose major events such as acquisitions, executive departures or bankruptcy, usually within four business days.

ww.An annual report that companies send to: An annual report to owners is the Form 10-K, a comprehensive yearly filing, whereas the Form 8-K is a short current report on specific events as they happen.
ww.A tax form for investors, filed to repor: Investors report gains on tax forms such as Schedule D and Form 1099-B, not Form 8-K, which is an SEC filing made by public companies and not by investors.
ww.A quarterly report that companies file e: The quarterly report filed every three months is the Form 10-Q, so this answer confuses it with the 8-K, which is filed only when a major event occurs.

rw: A proxy statement gives shareholders the information they need to vote on matters such as electing directors or approving pay at an annual meeting, either in person or by proxy.

ww.A statement of the company's profit for: The profit statement is the income statement in the annual report, not the proxy statement, which is focused on voting matters instead of profit and dividend mailings.
ww.A bill for broker fees that clients must: Broker fee bills are customer account statements and invoices from the brokerage, and they have no connection to the proxy statement a company sends to its shareholders.
ww.A list of the company's customers and th: A customer list with purchase amounts is internal sales data that companies generally keep private, and a proxy statement does not contain it, covering shareholder voting matters.

rw: A tender offer is a public offer to purchase shares directly from shareholders, usually at a premium over the market price, often used to take over a company or buy back stock.

ww.An offer to give shares away free to emp: Giving shares free to employees is a stock grant or award, not a tender offer, which is an offer to buy shares from existing shareholders, not give them away.
ww.An offer to sell bonds to the public by: Selling bonds to the public is a debt offering, which raises money for the issuer, whereas a tender offer is a buying offer made to current shareholders.
ww.An offer to lend money to a company at a: Lending money at a fixed rate is a loan or bond arrangement and is not a tender offer, which asks shareholders to sell their stock at a stated price.

rw: A hostile takeover is an acquisition that the target company's management opposes, so the bidder goes around the board by buying shares or appealing straight to the shareholders.

ww.A merger of two equals that both boards: A merger that both boards agree to is a friendly deal, and a hostile takeover is the opposite because the target's board and management do not support the acquisition.
ww.An acquisition both sides welcome and it: An acquisition that both sides welcome is a friendly takeover, not a hostile one, since hostility means the target's managers resist the buyer's bid rather than favor it.
ww.A sale of shares to the public by the co: A sale of shares to the public by founders is an offering or secondary sale, not a takeover, because no one is acquiring control of the company against resistance.

rw: A leveraged buyout buys a company using a large amount of borrowed money, often secured by the target's own assets, so debt rather than equity funds most of the purchase price.

ww.Buying a company using only cash on hand: Using only cash on hand is an all-cash purchase with no leverage, and the defining feature of a leveraged buyout is heavy borrowing instead of buying with cash alone.
ww.Buying a company with a government grant: A government grant or subsidy is not how a leveraged buyout is funded, since the buyer relies on debt financing from lenders and bond investors to complete the deal.
ww.Buying a company with the buyer's shares: Paying with the buyer's own shares and no loans is a stock-for-stock deal, which has no leverage, whereas a leveraged buyout relies on a large debt load.

rw: Merger arbitrage trades the shares of companies in a pending merger to profit from the gap between the current price and the deal price, accepting the risk the deal fails.

ww.Merging two stock exchanges into one tra: Merging exchanges into a single venue is an exchange consolidation, and it is unrelated to merger arbitrage, which is a trading strategy using price gaps between deal terms and market prices.
ww.Buying only bonds of firms that are abou: Merger arbitrage is not limited to bonds of firms about to merge, because it mainly involves trading the stocks of the companies in a deal to capture the spread.
ww.Splitting a company into two parts and s: Splitting a company into two parts and selling each is a divestiture or breakup, not merger arbitrage, which is a way for traders to profit from announced mergers.

rw: In a spin-off, a parent creates a new independent company by distributing its shares to existing shareholders, who then own stock in both the parent and the new company.

ww.A company going bankrupt and selling off: A company going bankrupt and selling assets to repay creditors is liquidation, which is very different from a spin-off, where a healthy company creates a new independent firm.
ww.Two companies combining into one larger: Two companies combining into a larger firm describes a merger, which is the opposite of a spin-off because a spin-off separates one company into two independent firms.
ww.A company buying back its own shares fro: Buying back shares on the open market is a repurchase that shrinks the share count, and it does not create a new independent company the way a spin-off does.

rw: An American depositary receipt lets U.S. investors buy and sell a foreign company's shares in dollars on U.S. exchanges, avoiding foreign brokers, currency exchange and overseas settlement difficulties.

ww.To fund foreign governments that need mo: Funding foreign governments for roads and schools is done through sovereign bonds and development lending, and ADRs are certificates tied to company shares, not government finance.
ww.To guarantee profits to U.S. investors w: No investment can guarantee profits, and an ADR carries the same market and currency risks as the underlying foreign shares, so guaranteeing returns is not its purpose.
ww.To avoid all taxes that foreign governme: ADR holders may still face foreign withholding taxes on dividends, so avoiding all taxes is not the purpose, which is easier access to foreign shares in U.S. dollars.

rw: Information technology has had the largest weight in the S&P 500 in recent years, driven by the big technology firms whose market values dominate the index, often above 25 percent.

ww.Utility and gas companies: Utilities make up only a small slice of the S&P 500, roughly 2 to 3 percent, far below the technology sector's weight, so they are not the largest sector.
ww.Materials and mining: Materials and mining companies account for only about 2 percent of the S&P 500 index, so they are one of the smallest sectors rather than the largest.
ww.Real estate stocks: Real estate is one of the smallest S&P 500 sectors at around 2 percent of the index, so it cannot be the sector with the largest weight.

rw: A 200-day moving average smooths daily prices over about 200 trading days, which shows the long-term trend direction of the stock and helps investors tell uptrends from downtrends.

ww.Showing the number of employees at the f: Employee counts are shown in company reports, not on a price chart, and a moving average is built from price data rather than from the number of workers.
ww.Showing the company's debts over time: Company debts are reported on the balance sheet, and a moving average of share prices does not measure borrowing, so it cannot show debts over time.
ww.Showing the next dividend payment date: Dividend payment dates are announced by the company's board and not derived from price averages, so a moving average cannot show when the next dividend is paid.

rw: A golden cross occurs when a short-term moving average, such as the 50-day, rises above a long-term one, such as the 200-day, which traders read as a bullish signal.

ww.When a short-term average falls below a: A short-term average falling below a long-term average is a death cross, which is bearish, so this describes the reverse of a golden cross.
ww.When a company pays a dividend that is h: A higher dividend than last year is a dividend increase and says nothing about moving averages, which are what define a golden cross on a price chart.
ww.When a stock hits a new low after a long: A stock that keeps hitting new lows after a long fall shows a persistent downtrend, which is bearish and unrelated to the bullish crossover of two averages.

rw: The RSI is a momentum indicator that compares recent average gains with recent average losses on a scale of 0 to 100, helping traders spot overbought or oversold conditions.

ww.A measure of dividends paid per share co: Dividends per share compared with price is the dividend yield, which measures income, whereas the relative strength index measures price momentum from recent gains and losses.
ww.A measure of a company's debt compared w: Debt compared with equity is the debt-to-equity ratio, a leverage measure from the balance sheet, not the RSI, which is calculated from price movements over a set period.
ww.A measure of a fund's fees compared with: Fund fees compared with similar funds is an expense ratio comparison, which has nothing to do with price momentum, and that is what the RSI actually measures.

rw: Overbought means the price has risen quickly and strongly, so the stock may be stretched and due for a pullback, a reading often shown by an RSI above 70.

ww.The company has too much debt and cannot: Too much debt describes financial distress or high leverage, which is a balance sheet problem and not what overbought means in technical analysis, a price-based concept.
ww.The company has too many shares outstand: Too many shares outstanding does not make a stock overbought, and extra shares would tend to dilute value, while overbought describes a sharp price run-up instead.
ww.The stock cannot be bought by any invest: Overbought does not mean the stock cannot be bought, since any investor can still place a buy order, and the term only signals that the price may be stretched.

rw: Free cash flow per share is $50 million divided by 25 million shares, which equals $2, so this option gives the correct figure from the stated numbers.

ww.$0.50: Getting $0.50 comes from dividing 25 by 50, which flips the fraction, whereas the correct calculation divides $50 million by 25 million shares to give $2 per share.
ww.$75: A figure of $75 results from adding 50 and 25, but per-share values come from division, and $50 million divided by 25 million shares equals $2, not $75.
ww.$1,250: A figure of $1,250 comes from multiplying 50 by 25, but per-share values require division, and $50 million divided by 25 million shares is $2, not $1,250.

rw: EV/EBITDA equals enterprise value divided by EBITDA, so $500 million divided by $50 million gives 10, meaning the company is valued at ten times its operating earnings.

ww.550: A multiple of 550 results from adding 500 and 50, but a multiple is a ratio, and $500 million divided by $50 million equals 10, not 550.
ww.0.1: A multiple of 0.1 comes from inverting the ratio, dividing 50 by 500, whereas EV/EBITDA places enterprise value on top, giving 500 divided by 50, which equals 10.
ww.25,000: A multiple of 25,000 results from multiplying 500 by 50, but a ratio needs division, and $500 million divided by $50 million is 10, not 25,000.

rw: A discounted cash flow analysis values an asset by estimating its expected future cash flows and discounting them back to present value using a rate that reflects the risk involved.

ww.Valuing an asset by its price on the las: The last trading day's market price is a quoted price, not a discounted cash flow valuation, which instead builds value from projected future cash flows and a discount rate.
ww.Valuing an asset by asking friends and r: Asking friends and relatives gives opinions rather than a measured valuation, whereas a DCF analysis uses explicit projections of future cash flows and a discount rate to derive worth.
ww.Valuing an asset by its logo and the col: A logo and brand colors have no bearing on financial value, and a DCF analysis focuses on cash flows and discounting, not on the look of the brand.

rw: Money today can be invested to earn interest, and inflation erodes the buying power of future dollars, which together explain the time value of money and why a dollar now is worth more.

ww.The government taxes future dollars at a: Tax rates on future dollars are not set differently from today's, so taxation is not the reason a dollar next year is worth less than a dollar now.
ww.Dollars lose their value on January 1 of: Dollars do not lose value on any particular date such as January 1, and the lower worth of future money comes from interest and inflation, not a calendar event.
ww.Banks refuse to hold future dollars for: Banks do not refuse to hold future dollars, since they accept deposits at any time, and the lower worth of future money reflects interest and inflation instead of bank policy.

rw: Present value equals $1,100 divided by 1.10, which is $1,000, so $1,000 invested at 10 percent for one year grows to exactly $1,100 and this answer is correct.

ww.$1,210: A figure of $1,210 multiplies $1,100 by 1.10 instead of dividing, which would give a future value, whereas present value divides by 1.10 to give $1,000.
ww.$990: A figure of $990 subtracts 10 percent of $1,100 from the amount, which is $110, but proper discounting divides by 1.10, giving $1,000 as the present value.
ww.$1,100: Using $1,100 ignores the discount rate, but money received in a year is worth less today, and dividing $1,100 by 1.10 produces a present value of $1,000.

rw: Future value equals $2,000 times 1.05 squared, which is $2,000 times 1.1025, giving $2,205, and the extra $5 above simple interest comes from interest earned on interest.

ww.$2,200: A figure of $2,200 uses simple interest at 10 percent total, but compounding for two years multiplies by 1.05 squared, which is 1.1025, giving $2,205 and not $2,200.
ww.$2,100: A figure of $2,100 only counts a single year of 5 percent growth, but two years of compounding is needed, giving $2,000 times 1.1025, or $2,205.
ww.$2,010: A figure of $2,010 applies only a fraction of the growth, while $2,000 times 1.05 times 1.05 equals $2,205, so two full years of compounding gives more.

rw: The PEG ratio equals the P/E ratio divided by expected earnings growth, which adjusts the valuation for growth so that fast-growing firms can be compared with slower ones fairly.

ww.The earnings per share divided by the pr: Earnings per share divided by price is the earnings yield, the inverse of the P/E ratio, whereas the PEG ratio divides the P/E ratio by the expected earnings growth rate.
ww.The price divided by the annual dividend: Price divided by annual dividend per share is the inverse of the dividend yield idea, and it has nothing to do with growth, which the PEG ratio specifically includes.
ww.The price divided by the total sales per: Price divided by sales per share is the price-to-sales ratio, a separate valuation measure, whereas the PEG ratio divides the P/E by expected earnings growth instead.

rw: The PEG ratio equals the P/E of 20 divided by expected earnings growth of 10 percent, which gives 2, so the stock trades at twice its growth rate.

ww.30: A figure of 30 comes from adding 20 and 10, but the PEG ratio divides, and 20 divided by 10 equals 2, so adding the numbers is wrong.
ww.200: A figure of 200 comes from multiplying 20 by 10, but PEG is a ratio calculated by division, so 20 divided by 10 equals 2, not 200.
ww.0.5: A figure of 0.5 comes from dividing 10 by 20, which inverts the formula, while the PEG ratio puts the P/E on top, giving 20 divided by 10, or 2.

rw: The price-to-sales ratio equals market capitalization divided by total sales, or equivalently price per share divided by sales per share, so it shows what investors pay per dollar of revenue.

ww.Price divided by the earnings per share: Price divided by earnings per share is the P/E ratio, which looks at profits, whereas the price-to-sales ratio compares market value with revenue instead of earnings.
ww.Price divided by book value per share of: Price divided by book value per share is the price-to-book ratio, which uses equity on the balance sheet, not the sales figure that the price-to-sales ratio uses.
ww.Total sales divided by the price per sha: Total sales divided by price per share turns the ratio upside down, since price-to-sales puts the market value on top and sales on the bottom, not the reverse.

rw: Price-to-book equals the $30 price divided by $15 book value per share, which is 2, meaning the market values the equity at twice its accounting value.

ww.45: A figure of 45 comes from adding 30 and 15, but a ratio divides, and $30 divided by $15 equals 2, not 45.
ww.450: A figure of 450 comes from multiplying 30 by 15, but price-to-book requires division, and $30 divided by $15 equals 2, not 450.
ww.0.5: A figure of 0.5 inverts the ratio by dividing 15 by 30, but price-to-book puts the price on top, so $30 divided by $15 gives 2.

rw: Operating margin equals operating income divided by revenue, showing the share of each sales dollar left after operating costs but before interest and taxes are subtracted.

ww.Total debt divided by total equity: Total debt divided by total equity is the debt-to-equity ratio, which measures leverage, whereas the operating margin measures how much operating profit a company earns on each dollar of revenue.
ww.Revenue divided by net income earned: Revenue divided by net income turns the margin upside down, since a margin puts profit on top and revenue below, and this also uses net income, not operating income.
ww.Net income divided by total assets: Net income divided by total assets is return on assets, which measures how well assets generate profit, and it is a different ratio from operating margin.

rw: Operating margin equals $60 million of operating income divided by $400 million of revenue, which is 0.15 or 15 percent, so the company keeps 15 cents per dollar of sales.

ww.460 percent: A figure of 460 percent adds revenue and operating income, but margin divides operating income by revenue, so $60 million divided by $400 million equals 15 percent.
ww.6.7 percent: A figure of 6.7 percent inverts the usual comparison by dividing 400 by 60 and cutting it incorrectly, but $60 million divided by $400 million gives 15 percent.
ww.1.5 percent: A figure of 1.5 percent is off by a factor of ten, because $60 million divided by $400 million is 0.15, which is 15 percent and not 1.5 percent.

rw: The interest coverage ratio equals operating income divided by interest expense, showing how many times a company can pay its interest from earnings, so higher numbers signal safer debt.

ww.Revenue divided by total assets of the f: Revenue divided by total assets is asset turnover, which shows how efficiently assets create sales, and it says nothing about the ability to cover interest payments.
ww.Net income divided by the dividends paid: Net income divided by dividends paid relates to the dividend payout and coverage of dividends, not to interest expense, which is what the coverage ratio measures.
ww.Total debt divided by the firm's total e: Total debt divided by total equity is the debt-to-equity ratio, a leverage measure, whereas interest coverage compares operating earnings with the interest cost on the debt.

rw: Interest coverage equals operating income of $12 million divided by interest expense of $3 million, which is 4, so earnings cover the interest cost four times over.

ww.15: A figure of 15 adds 12 and 3, but coverage is found by dividing operating income by interest expense, so $12 million divided by $3 million equals 4.
ww.36: A figure of 36 comes from multiplying 12 by 3, but coverage is a ratio, and $12 million divided by $3 million equals 4, not 36.
ww.0.25: A figure of 0.25 inverts the formula by dividing 3 by 12, but coverage puts operating income on top, so $12 million divided by $3 million equals 4.

rw: A high debt-to-equity ratio shows the company relies heavily on borrowed money, which raises financial risk because fixed interest and principal payments must be met in bad times too.

ww.The company has no debt and so it carrie: A high debt-to-equity ratio means debt is large compared with equity, so claiming the company has no debt and carries no financial risk contradicts what the ratio measures.
ww.The company is certain to grow, as a fir: Debt does not make growth certain, and a high ratio raises risk because interest must be paid whether or not the projects succeed, so it guarantees nothing.
ww.The company pays no taxes because its de: Interest deductions lower taxable income, but they do not eliminate all taxes, and the ratio is a measure of leverage and risk, not a measure of tax payments.

rw: Working capital equals current assets minus current liabilities, so it shows the short-term liquidity cushion available for paying bills that fall due within the next year.

ww.Total assets minus total liabilities ove: Total assets minus total liabilities is equity or net worth, a broader measure, while working capital looks only at the current items that support short-term operations.
ww.Cash on hand minus all the debt owed: Cash minus all debt is net cash or net debt, which mixes long-term obligations in, whereas working capital compares all current assets with only current liabilities.
ww.Revenue minus all the expenses paid: Revenue minus expenses is profit or net income, which measures performance over a period, and it is not working capital, which measures short-term liquidity on the balance sheet.

rw: Working capital equals current assets of $800,000 minus current liabilities of $500,000, which is $300,000, so the firm has that much cushion for short-term obligations.

ww.$500,000: A figure of $500,000 only repeats the current liabilities, but working capital subtracts them from current assets of $800,000, leaving $300,000.
ww.$1.6: A figure of $1.6 is the ratio of 800,000 divided by 500,000, which is the current ratio, but working capital is a dollar difference of $300,000.
ww.$1,300,000: A figure of $1,300,000 adds the two numbers, but working capital subtracts liabilities from assets, so $800,000 minus $500,000 equals $300,000.

rw: The current ratio equals current assets of $800,000 divided by current liabilities of $500,000, which is 1.6, meaning the firm has $1.60 of current assets for each $1 owed.

ww.13: A figure of 13 mixes up the numbers by adding 800 and 500, but a ratio requires division, and $800,000 divided by $500,000 equals 1.6.
ww.300,000: A figure of 300,000 is the working capital difference in dollars, but the current ratio divides current assets by current liabilities, giving $800,000 divided by $500,000, or 1.6.
ww.0.625: A figure of 0.625 inverts the ratio by dividing liabilities by assets, but the current ratio puts current assets on top, so $800,000 divided by $500,000 is 1.6.

rw: The quick ratio divides liquid current assets, such as cash, receivables and securities, excluding inventory, by current liabilities, giving a stricter test of ability to pay near-term bills.

ww.Net income divided by sales for the full: Net income divided by sales is the net profit margin, a profitability ratio, whereas the quick ratio measures short-term liquidity by comparing liquid assets with current liabilities.
ww.All assets divided by all liabilities, i: All assets divided by all liabilities includes inventory and buildings, which are not quickly turned into cash, so it is not the quick ratio, which uses only liquid assets.
ww.Total debt divided by total equity of th: Total debt divided by total equity is the debt-to-equity ratio, which measures leverage over the long term, not the short-term liquidity that the quick ratio is designed to test.

rw: Inventory turnover measures how many times a company sells and replaces its inventory during a period, which shows how efficiently stock is managed and how fast goods move.

ww.How long a firm has existed since it was: How long a firm has existed is its age or track record, and it has no connection to inventory turnover, which tracks how fast goods are sold.
ww.How much profit a firm makes on each sal: Profit made on each sale is the profit margin, which looks at earnings per sale, whereas inventory turnover looks at how many times stock is sold and replaced.
ww.How much inventory a firm owns on the la: Inventory owned on the last day of the year is a balance sheet amount, a single static figure, and it does not show how often stock is sold and replaced.

rw: DuPont analysis breaks return on equity into profit margin, asset turnover and financial leverage, which shows whether ROE comes from profitability, efficiency or borrowing, and where it might be improved.

ww.A tax calculation that shows what share: A tax calculation showing the share of income paid to the state is an effective tax rate idea, whereas DuPont analysis breaks down return on equity into its component drivers.
ww.Splitting a stock into pieces so that ea: Splitting a stock so each share costs less is a stock split, a corporate action, and it is unrelated to DuPont analysis, which is a way to analyze ROE.
ww.A chemical test used to find traces of a: DuPont analysis is a financial method and not a chemical test, even though it is named after the DuPont company, where the technique was developed in the early 1900s.

rw: EBITDA stands for earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization, a measure of operating profit that ignores financing, tax and noncash charges and helps compare companies.

ww.Total equity, the owners' stake in the n: Total equity is the owners' stake in net assets on the balance sheet, which is a different concept from EBITDA, an earnings measure taken from the income statement.
ww.Earnings after all expenses and taxes, t: Earnings after all expenses and taxes is net income, the bottom line, whereas EBITDA adds back interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization to show operating performance.
ww.Total revenue, which is all the money a: Total revenue is the top line, all money from sales before any expenses, while EBITDA subtracts operating costs and adds back certain items, so it is much lower.

rw: A moat is a durable competitive advantage, such as a strong brand, patents or low costs, that protects a company's profits from competitors over many years.

ww.A ditch around its headquarters, dug to: A moat is a metaphor used in investing, not a ditch around headquarters, and it refers to a company's business advantage rather than any physical barrier for visitors.
ww.Its total debt, which is the sum of all: Total debt is the sum of loans and bonds owed, which is a liability, and it is not a moat, which is an advantage that protects profits.
ww.Its tax bill, which is the amount owed t: A tax bill is an amount owed to the government and does not protect the business from competitors, so it is not what investors mean by a moat.

rw: A margin of safety means buying at a price below the estimated intrinsic value, so errors in the estimate and bad luck are less likely to cause a loss.

ww.Using borrowed money to buy more shares: Using borrowed money to buy more shares than you can afford is leverage, which adds risk, whereas a margin of safety lowers risk by requiring a discount.
ww.Buying only at the highest price, as thi: Buying only at the highest price does the opposite of a margin of safety, because paying more than value leaves no cushion against mistakes or declines.
ww.Selling when prices fall to avoid any mo: Selling after prices fall is a stop-loss style action, not a margin of safety, which is about the discount at purchase and not about when you sell.

rw: CAPM links an asset's expected return to its systematic risk measured by beta, using the risk-free rate plus beta times the market risk premium, so this option describes it correctly.

ww.A model for tax filing that helps people: CAPM is a financial model for expected returns and is not used for tax filing, which relies on tax rules, forms and deadlines rather than risk and return.
ww.A model for setting bank interest rates: Bank interest rates on loans and deposits are set using central bank policy and competition, whereas CAPM estimates the return investors require on a risky asset.
ww.A model for pricing houses based on size: Pricing houses by size, location and age describes a hedonic valuation approach, not CAPM, which relates expected asset returns to market risk measured by beta.

rw: CAPM gives 3 percent plus 1.5 times the 6 percent market premium, which is 3 plus 9, or 12 percent, so the stock's higher beta earns a higher required return.

ww.4.5 percent: A figure of 4.5 percent is only beta times the 3 percent risk-free rate, but CAPM uses the 6 percent market premium, giving 3 plus 1.5 times 6, or 12 percent.
ww.13.5 percent: A figure of 13.5 percent multiplies beta by the 9 percent market return instead of the 6 percent premium, whereas CAPM gives 3 plus 1.5 times 6, or 12 percent.
ww.9 percent: A figure of 9 percent is just the market return, which would apply to a beta of 1, but this stock has beta 1.5 and so should return 12 percent.

rw: Alpha is the excess return of an investment relative to its benchmark after adjusting for risk, so a positive alpha means the manager added value beyond what the market risk explains.

ww.The first letter of the Greek alphabet,: Alpha is the first Greek letter, but in investing it means something specific, the excess return versus a benchmark, so a logo or club name is not the meaning.
ww.The size of a company measured by the nu: Company size measured by employees has nothing to do with alpha, which measures a manager's or investment's risk-adjusted performance relative to a benchmark rather than how large the firm is.
ww.The beginning price of a stock at the ti: A beginning price at first listing is an initial offering price and is not alpha, which measures how much an investment outperforms its risk-adjusted benchmark return.

rw: A correlation of +1 means the two assets move perfectly together in direction and proportion, so holding both gives no diversification benefit when one of them falls.

ww.They are unrelated to each other: A correlation of 0 means two assets are unrelated, whereas +1 is the maximum value, so describing them as unrelated confuses zero correlation with perfect positive correlation.
ww.They never change in value: Correlation measures how assets move relative to each other, not whether their values change, and two assets can both change a great deal and still show +1 correlation.
ww.They move in opposite directions: Moving in opposite directions describes a negative correlation, with perfect opposite movement being -1, so it is the reverse of what a +1 correlation means.

rw: Assets with low or negative correlation tend not to fall at the same time, so combining them reduces the portfolio's overall risk, which gives the greatest diversification benefit.

ww.Two shares of the same company and secto: Two shares of the same company and sector are highly correlated and share the same risks, so they provide very little diversification when the sector or firm declines.
ww.Two funds tracking the same index closel: Two funds tracking the same index closely hold nearly identical stocks, so their returns are almost perfectly correlated and combining them adds almost no diversification benefit.
ww.Two stocks in the same industry and coun: Two stocks in the same industry and country face the same economic and sector risks, so they tend to move together and diversify poorly compared with unrelated assets.

rw: Standard deviation measures how much returns vary around their average, so a higher figure means more volatility and uncertainty, which is why investors use it as a measure of risk.

ww.The total fees paid by the fund to its m: Total fees paid to a manager are measured by the expense ratio and dollar charges, not by standard deviation, which describes the volatility of returns around the average.
ww.The average return of a fund over the ye: The average return over the years is the mean, and standard deviation measures the spread around that mean, not the mean itself, so this describes a different statistic.
ww.The number of holdings in a fund or a po: The number of holdings in a fund is a count of securities and is unrelated to standard deviation, which measures the variability of returns, not the size of the portfolio.

rw: Fund A ranges from -10 to +30 percent, a 40 point spread, much wider than Fund B's 6 point spread, so Fund A has the higher standard deviation.

ww.Equal: The two funds do not have equal standard deviations, since Fund A swings across a 40 point range while Fund B moves across only 6 points.
ww.Neither: Both funds have returns that vary, and a standard deviation is always greater than zero when returns differ, so saying neither has a higher figure is wrong.
ww.Fund B: Fund B varies only between 2 and 8 percent, a range of 6 points, which is far narrower than Fund A's 40 point range, so Fund B has the lower figure.

rw: A drawdown is the decline from a peak in value to a subsequent trough, which shows how much an investor would have lost at the worst point.

ww.A bond's maturity date when principal is: A bond's maturity date is when principal is repaid, which is a repayment event and not a drawdown, which measures a fall in value from a peak.
ww.A fee charged by a broker for each trade: A fee charged by a broker for each trade is a commission, which is a cost, whereas a drawdown measures how far an investment has fallen from a prior high.
ww.A withdrawal from an account made by the: A withdrawal from an account by its owner is a cash distribution, which is different from a drawdown, a measure of investment loss from peak to trough.

rw: The Treynor ratio equals excess return over the risk-free rate divided by beta, so it measures return per unit of systematic risk, which is what this option says.

ww.Return per dollar of fees paid to the fu: Return per dollar of fees paid is a cost-effectiveness idea, not the Treynor ratio, which divides excess return by beta, the measure of market risk.
ww.Excess return per unit of total risk mea: Excess return per unit of total risk measured by sigma is the Sharpe ratio, which uses standard deviation, whereas the Treynor ratio uses beta as its measure of risk.
ww.Return per share of stock held in the fu: Return per share held is not a risk-adjusted measure, and the Treynor ratio instead compares excess return over the risk-free rate with the investment's beta.

rw: Earnings yield equals earnings per share divided by price, which is the inverse of the P/E ratio, and shows the percentage of the price that the company earns each year.

ww.Dividends divided by price per share: Dividends divided by price per share is the dividend yield, which measures income, whereas the earnings yield divides earnings per share by price and so measures profit relative to price.
ww.Price divided by earnings per share: Price divided by earnings per share is the P/E ratio, which is the inverse of the earnings yield, so this option flips the fraction upside down.
ww.Total sales divided by price per share: Total sales divided by price per share is the inverse of the price-to-sales ratio, and it uses revenue rather than earnings, so it is not the earnings yield.

rw: Earnings yield is the inverse of the P/E, so 1 divided by 25 equals 0.04 or 4 percent, which means the stock earns 4 cents per dollar of price.

ww.50 percent: A figure of 50 percent comes from multiplying 25 by 2, but earnings yield is the inverse of the P/E, so 1 divided by 25 equals 4 percent.
ww.2.5 percent: A figure of 2.5 percent divides 25 by 10 instead of inverting it, but the earnings yield is 1 divided by the P/E of 25, which equals 4 percent.
ww.25 percent: A figure of 25 percent just reuses the P/E number, but a P/E of 25 means the yield is its inverse, 1 divided by 25, or 4 percent.

rw: Total return equals price gain plus dividend over the starting price, so $5 plus $2 is $7, and $7 divided by $50 equals 14 percent.

ww.10 percent: A figure of 10 percent counts only the price gain of $5 on $50 and ignores the $2 dividend, so total return is higher than 10 percent.
ww.4 percent: A figure of 4 percent counts only the $2 dividend over $50 and leaves out the $5 price gain, so it omits most of the return.
ww.7 percent: A figure of 7 percent uses the $7 combined gain but divides by 100 instead of the $50 starting price, whereas $7 divided by $50 equals 14 percent.

rw: A 20 percent gain makes 1.20 and a 20 percent loss then leaves 0.80 of that, so 1.20 times 0.80 equals 0.96, a loss of about 4 percent.

ww.Break-even, as both offset: Break-even is wrong because the 20 percent loss applies to a larger base after the gain, so 1.20 times 0.80 equals 0.96, not 1.00, and a loss results.
ww.A gain of about 4 percent: A gain of 4 percent has the sign reversed, since 1.20 times 0.80 equals 0.96, which is below 1.00, so the portfolio ends lower than it started.
ww.A loss of about 40 percent: A loss of 40 percent adds the two 20 percent losses wrongly, but the gain comes first, so the result is 1.20 times 0.80, or 0.96, a 4 percent loss.

rw: The geometric average return measures the compound growth rate over multiple periods, so it accounts for the effect of compounding and volatility, which a simple arithmetic average ignores.

ww.Measuring the total size of a portfolio: The total size of a portfolio at a single date is its value in dollars, which is a point-in-time measure and not a growth rate across periods like the geometric average.
ww.Measuring the highest return in a single: The highest return in a single year is a maximum figure picked from the record, whereas the geometric average blends all years into one compound rate of growth.
ww.Measuring the total fees paid to the fun: Fees paid to a manager and broker are costs measured in dollars or percent of assets, and the geometric average return measures growth rather than the cost of management.

rw: Growth compounds, so the total return is 1.10 times 1.20, which equals 1.32, or 32 percent, and the extra 2 points come from the second year's gain on year one's gain.

ww.30 percent: A figure of 30 percent simply adds 10 and 20, but returns compound, so 1.10 times 1.20 equals 1.32, which means a 32 percent total two-year return.
ww.200 percent: A figure of 200 percent multiplies 10 by 20, which has no meaning here, because the total two-year return is found by compounding, 1.10 times 1.20 equals 1.32, or 32 percent.
ww.15 percent: A figure of 15 percent averages the two returns, but that is an average and not the total, and compounding gives 1.10 times 1.20, or 32 percent in all.

rw: Present value equals $50,000 divided by 1.05 to the tenth power, which is about 1.629, giving roughly $30,700, so she needs to invest about that amount today.

ww.About $50,000: Investing $50,000 today would grow to about $81,400 in 10 years at 5 percent, far above the goal, so she needs to invest much less than the target.
ww.About $75,000: Investing $75,000 would grow to more than $122,000 in 10 years, which is well above the $50,000 goal, and discounting always gives a present value below the target.
ww.About $25,000: Investing $25,000 would grow to only about $40,700 at 5 percent for 10 years, short of $50,000, so she needs about $30,700 instead.

rw: Shares of a large company on a major exchange can be sold in seconds at a visible price, with heavy volume, so they are generally the most liquid choice here.

ww.A 10-year CD with a penalty for early wi: A 10-year CD carries a penalty for early withdrawal, so cashing it out costs money and time, which makes it much less liquid than a listed share.
ww.A piece of real estate in a growing town: Real estate takes weeks or months to market and close, and transaction costs are high, so it is far less liquid than a large listed stock.
ww.A share of a private business that is no: Shares of a private business are not listed, so there is no ready market, and finding a buyer takes time, which makes them less liquid than listed stock.

rw: A parcel of land can take months to sell, needs appraisals and legal work and has no continuous market, so it is generally the least liquid of these options.

ww.Large listed stock: Large listed stock can be sold within seconds on an exchange at a visible price, making it among the most liquid assets, not the least liquid.
ww.A savings account: A savings account allows withdrawal on demand at full value, which makes it highly liquid, so it is not the least liquid choice here.
ww.A money market fund: A money market fund can usually be redeemed within a day at a stable value, so it is highly liquid and not the least liquid of these choices.

rw: An investment policy statement sets out the investor's goals, risk tolerance and limits, and strategy, giving a written plan that guides decisions and helps avoid emotional mistakes.

ww.To forecast where market prices go next: Forecasting market prices with accuracy is not possible for any document, and an investment policy statement does not predict prices, so this is not its purpose.
ww.To list the broker's fees and the commis: Listing broker fees and commissions is a job for a fee schedule or account agreement, not for an investment policy statement, which is a plan for the portfolio.
ww.To guarantee a fixed return on every inv: No document can guarantee a fixed return on every investment, since returns depend on markets, and an investment policy statement only sets the goals and rules for investing.

rw: Realized losses offset gains, so $5,000 of gains minus $3,000 of losses leaves a net taxable gain of $2,000, which is the amount taxed.

ww.$3,000: A net gain of $3,000 uses only the losses figure, but netting means subtracting $3,000 of losses from $5,000 of gains, leaving $2,000 as the taxable amount.
ww.$8,000: A figure of $8,000 adds gains and losses together, but realized losses offset gains, so $5,000 minus $3,000 equals $2,000, not $8,000.
ww.$5,000: A figure of $5,000 ignores the $3,000 of realized losses, but those losses reduce the taxable gain, so the net amount is $5,000 minus $3,000, or $2,000.

rw: A traditional IRA defers tax on the interest until withdrawal, so the high taxable interest from a bond fund is sheltered each year, making it the best location.

ww.A checking account at a local retail ban: A checking account at a bank cannot hold a bond fund, and it earns little interest, so it is not a suitable place for a high-yield bond fund.
ww.A taxable brokerage account with no tax: A taxable brokerage account would tax the bond fund's interest each year at ordinary rates, which is costly, so it is a worse home than a tax-deferred account.
ww.A cash drawer in a store's front checkou: A cash drawer at a store is not an investment account and cannot hold a fund, so it makes no sense as a place for a bond fund.

rw: A broad stock index fund has low turnover and mostly qualified dividends and long-term gains, so it is already tax-efficient and works well in a taxable account.

ww.A REIT held for its rents: A REIT pays most income as dividends that are largely taxed at ordinary rates, so it is tax-inefficient and better held in a tax-deferred account.
ww.A high-yield bond fund: A high-yield bond fund pays interest that is taxed at ordinary income rates each year, which makes it tax-inefficient and better suited to a tax-deferred account.
ww.A fund with high turnover: A fund with high turnover creates frequent short-term gains that are taxed at higher ordinary rates, so it is tax-inefficient and a poor fit for a taxable account.

rw: Asset location means deciding which accounts, such as taxable, tax-deferred or tax-free, hold which investments, so that tax-heavy assets sit in sheltered accounts and boost after-tax returns.

ww.Choosing which broker's office to visit: Choosing a broker's office to visit is about convenience and service, not about taxes, and asset location refers to the type of account that holds each investment.
ww.Choosing the country where an investor l: The country where an investor lives sets tax rules, but that is residence and not asset location, which means choosing which account type holds which investment.
ww.Choosing which bank branch to use for op: Choosing a bank branch for a checking account is a convenience decision with no link to asset location, which concerns where to hold investments for tax efficiency.

rw: In a target-date fund the glide path is the planned shift from stocks toward safer assets like bonds as the target retirement date nears, which lowers risk with age.

ww.The path a plane takes when it descends: A plane's descent path is a different meaning of glide path, and in a target-date fund the term refers to how the asset mix changes over time.
ww.The path of a stock price over the cours: The path of a stock price over a year is a price chart or history and is not the glide path, which is a plan for the fund's asset mix.
ww.The route to the broker's office that th: The route a client drives to a broker's office has nothing to do with investing, and the glide path in a fund describes its changing mix of assets.

rw: Time horizon, the years until the money is needed, strongly shapes how much risk a portfolio can take, so a 35-year-old can hold more stocks than a 65-year-old.

ww.Zip code: A zip code does not determine the right asset mix, because investing decisions depend on goals, risk capacity and time, not on where a person lives.
ww.Hair color: Hair color has no bearing on how a portfolio should be built, and the difference between the two investors comes from their time horizons instead.
ww.Favorite sports: Favorite sports have no relation to financial planning, and the real reason the portfolios differ is that one investor has decades to recover from losses and the other does not.

rw: Sequence-of-returns risk is the danger that poor returns early in retirement hurt more than later ones, because withdrawals during a downturn shrink the base that must recover and grow.

ww.The risk that interest rates rise and cu: The risk that rising rates cut bond prices is interest rate risk, which is a different risk from sequence-of-returns risk, about the order in which returns come.
ww.The risk of making too many trades in a: Making too many trades creates costs and taxes, but that is turnover or trading risk, not sequence-of-returns risk, which concerns the timing of gains and losses.
ww.The risk of losing a sequence number tha: A lost file sequence number is a data record problem and has nothing to do with investing, and sequence-of-returns risk is about the order of investment returns.

rw: The 4 percent rule suggests withdrawing about 4 percent of the portfolio in the first year of retirement and then adjusting that dollar amount for inflation each following year.

ww.A rule that says taxes on retirement wit: The 4 percent rule is a withdrawal guideline and not a tax cap, since taxes on retirement withdrawals depend on account type and the rates that apply, not a flat 4 percent.
ww.A rule that says stocks must rise at lea: The 4 percent rule does not set a minimum stock gain before selling, because it is a spending guideline for retirees and does not restrict when investors may sell shares.
ww.A rule that limits the fees a fund may c: The 4 percent rule does not limit fund fees, which are set by the funds and disclosed in the prospectus, since the rule is about how much retirees can withdraw each year.

rw: The 4 percent rule gives $800,000 times 0.04, which equals $32,000 for the first year, and she can adjust that amount for inflation in later years.

ww.$3,200: A figure of $3,200 is 0.4 percent of $800,000, a decimal slip, but 4 percent of $800,000 is $32,000, which is the correct first-year withdrawal.
ww.$320,000: A figure of $320,000 is 40 percent of $800,000, ten times too large, whereas 4 percent of $800,000 equals $32,000, which is a sustainable first-year withdrawal.
ww.$80,000: A figure of $80,000 is 10 percent of $800,000, far above the 4 percent rule, and 4 percent of $800,000 is $32,000, so that withdrawal would drain savings quickly.

rw: Longevity risk is the risk of outliving one's savings, because a longer life means more years of spending that the retirement portfolio has to fund.

ww.The risk that a stock lasts too long: Longevity risk has nothing to do with a stock lasting too long, and it concerns a person living longer than expected and running out of money.
ww.The risk of a short trading day: A short trading day is a market schedule matter and has no connection to a person's lifespan, which is what longevity risk is about.
ww.The risk that a bond matures too soon: A bond maturing too soon is reinvestment risk, a different concept, whereas longevity risk is the chance that a retiree lives longer than the money lasts.

rw: An annuity pays income for life, so it transfers the risk of outliving savings to the insurer and directly addresses longevity risk for the retiree.

ww.A single speculative growth stock: A single speculative growth stock adds volatility and does not provide a guaranteed income stream, so it does not help address the risk of outliving savings.
ww.A one-year certificate of deposit: A one-year certificate of deposit matures quickly and offers only a limited, short-term return, so it does not secure income for life.
ww.A checking account with no interest: A checking account with no interest loses buying power to inflation and provides no lifetime income, so it does not help with longevity risk.

rw: Form CRS is a short relationship summary that broker-dealers and investment advisers give retail investors, explaining services, fees, conflicts of interest and disciplinary history in plain language.

ww.A tax form that employers use to report: A tax form used by employers to report wages is the W-2, and Form CRS is not a tax form but a disclosure document given to retail investors.
ww.A loan application that borrowers fill i: A mortgage loan application is filled in by borrowers for lenders, which is a different document altogether from Form CRS, a disclosure given to investors.
ww.A brokerage statement that lists an inve: A monthly brokerage statement lists holdings and activity, whereas Form CRS is a short summary of the firm's services and fees, not an account statement.

rw: Form ADV is the registration document investment advisers file, and it discloses their business, fees, conflicts of interest and disciplinary history, so clients can evaluate the adviser.

ww.A stock certificate showing that a perso: A stock certificate shows ownership of shares, and Form ADV is not a certificate but the registration and disclosure document that investment advisers file with regulators.
ww.A tax form that investors file each year: A tax form reporting gains and losses to the IRS is Schedule D or Form 8949, not Form ADV, which is filed by advisers to register with regulators.
ww.A mutual fund prospectus that explains t: A mutual fund prospectus explains a fund's goals, risks and costs, whereas Form ADV describes an investment adviser's business, fees and conflicts and is not about a fund.

rw: An accredited investor meets income or net-worth thresholds set by the SEC, so regulators treat the person as able to bear the risk of private offerings.

ww.An investor under 18 years of age who ho: A minor holding an account through a parent is not an accredited investor, because accreditation depends on income or net worth and not on age or custodial status.
ww.An investor who has passed a school exam: Passing a school exam in economics does not make someone accredited, because the status is set by income or net-worth tests or certain licenses, not by schooling.
ww.An investor who works at a bank or in th: Working in the financial industry in any role does not make someone accredited, since status depends on income, net worth or specific licenses, not on a job at a bank.

rw: A private placement is a sale of securities directly to a limited group of investors, not the general public, and it usually avoids full SEC registration under an exemption.

ww.A government bond auction held by the Tr: A Treasury bond auction is a public sale of government debt, which is different from a private placement, a sale of securities to a limited group of investors.
ww.A public sale of shares on an exchange,: A public sale of shares on an exchange open to any investor is a public offering, which is the opposite of a private placement made to a few.
ww.A bank loan made to a company by a lende: A bank loan repaid with interest is a lending arrangement and is not a sale of securities, which is what a private placement involves.

rw: Rule 144 is an SEC rule that sets conditions, such as holding periods and volume limits, for reselling restricted or control securities to the public without registration.

ww.A rule that bans all trading in a stock: A rule stopping all trading in a stock after a sharp drop describes circuit breakers or the limit-up, limit-down rules, not Rule 144, which covers resale of restricted securities.
ww.A rule for bank deposits that sets how m: Rules on how much a depositor may insure at one bank are FDIC deposit insurance rules, and they have nothing to do with the SEC's Rule 144.
ww.A rule that sets the price of shares on: Exchanges do not set share prices each morning by regulatory rule, because prices come from trading, and Rule 144 deals with when restricted securities may be resold.

rw: Rule 10b-5 is an SEC rule that prohibits fraud, misleading statements and manipulation in connection with buying or selling securities, and it is the basis for many insider trading cases.

ww.A rule on stock splits that sets how man: A rule on stock splits and issuing new shares is a corporate matter and is not Rule 10b-5, which targets fraud and manipulation in securities trading.
ww.A rule on bank reserves that sets the sh: Bank reserve requirements are set by the Federal Reserve and have nothing to do with Rule 10b-5, which is an antifraud rule under the securities laws.
ww.A rule setting tax rates that the Treasu: Tax rates on investment gains are set by Congress and the Treasury and IRS, and Rule 10b-5 is an SEC antifraud rule that does not set any tax rate.

rw: Market manipulation means intentionally interfering with the free market to create a false or misleading price, such as through wash trades, spoofing or spreading false rumors, and it is illegal.

ww.Researching a company thoroughly before: Researching a company before buying is ordinary due diligence and is encouraged, since it does not interfere with the market or create any false price.
ww.Trading a stock at a profit after the pr: Selling a stock at a profit after good news is normal, lawful trading, and it involves no deception or artificial pricing of the shares.
ww.Holding stock for many years while the c: Holding stock for years while a company grows is long-term investing, a lawful strategy that does not distort prices or mislead other traders in the market.

rw: Spoofing means placing orders with no intention to execute them, typically canceling before they fill, to mislead other traders about supply and demand and move the price.

ww.Posting a stock tip on a public forum af: Posting a tip after doing your own research is ordinary speech and is not spoofing, which is the placing of orders you do not mean to execute.
ww.Making a joke about a stock in a post th: Making an obvious joke about a stock misleads no one, whereas spoofing is deceptive because the orders placed are meant to fool other traders about demand.
ww.Canceling a trade for a good reason, suc: Canceling a trade for a good reason, such as a pricing mistake, is legitimate, whereas spoofing involves entering orders with the intent to cancel them to deceive others.

rw: The Series 65 is the Uniform Investment Adviser Law exam, which qualifies people as investment adviser representatives, so this is the license it describes.

ww.A license to practice law in the courts: Practicing law in state courts requires a law degree and passing the bar, not a Series 65, which is a securities licensing exam for advisers.
ww.A license to run a bank branch or a savi: Running a bank branch is a banking management job with no Series 65 requirement, because that exam covers securities and investment advice, not banking.
ww.A license to sell cars at a dealership i: Selling cars at a dealership requires a state dealer license, not a securities license, and the Series 65 relates to investment advice instead.

rw: The Series 63 is the Uniform Securities Agent State Law exam, which many states require for registered representatives who sell securities within their borders.

ww.A real estate exam taken by agents who w: A real estate exam for agents is a different state licensing test, and the Series 63 covers securities law, not selling homes.
ww.A mutual fund exam taken by people who w: Managing mutual funds is not what the Series 63 licenses, since it tests knowledge of state securities law for representatives rather than fund management.
ww.A federal tax exam taken by people who w: Preparing tax returns involves IRS and state credentials, not the Series 63, which is a securities exam, so a tax exam is the wrong match.

rw: CFP stands for Certified Financial Planner, a credential for financial planners who meet education, exam, experience and ethics requirements set by the CFP Board.

ww.Customer Fee Plan, a credential for clie: The CFP designation does not stand for a customer fee plan, and the credential is for financial planners, not for clients negotiating lower charges.
ww.Certified Fund Pool, a credential for pe: CFP does not stand for Certified Fund Pool, and the credential certifies financial planners, not people who manage investment pools.
ww.Chartered Fraud Prevention, a credential: CFP does not mean Chartered Fraud Prevention, and fraud investigators hold other credentials, such as the Certified Fraud Examiner, while the CFP is for planning.

rw: The CFA charter means Chartered Financial Analyst, a professional credential in investment analysis earned by passing three exam levels and meeting experience requirements.

ww.A charter for a broker, giving a firm th: The CFA charter is not a license for a brokerage firm to trade for clients, because it is a professional credential earned by an individual, not a firm.
ww.A charter for a bank, granted by a regul: A bank charter is granted by a regulator to allow deposit taking, which is a different meaning of the word, and the CFA charter is a personal credential.
ww.A charter for a stock exchange, granted: A stock exchange charter is granted to founders by government, which has nothing to do with the CFA charter, a credential earned by passing exams.

rw: BrokerCheck is a free FINRA tool that lets investors look up the background, licenses, employment history and disciplinary record of brokers and brokerage firms.

ww.A tool for trading stocks that lets inve: BrokerCheck is not a trading tool, since investors cannot place orders from a phone with it, and it is a lookup service for background information.
ww.A tool for tax filing that helps people: BrokerCheck is not a tool for tax filing, and it does not help people prepare or submit returns, because it provides information on brokers and firms.
ww.A tool for paying brokers that lets clie: BrokerCheck does not pay brokers, and clients cannot send fees to advisers through it, since it only provides records about registered professionals.

rw: EDGAR is the SEC's Electronic Data Gathering, Analysis and Retrieval database, where public company filings such as 10-Ks, 10-Qs and 8-Ks are available to the public.

ww.A credit bureau that tracks the borrowin: A credit bureau tracking consumer borrowing is Equifax, Experian or TransUnion, not EDGAR, which is the SEC's database of public company filings.
ww.A trading platform where investors place: EDGAR is not a trading platform for placing orders, since it only provides filings and does not execute trades for investors.
ww.A stock exchange where listed companies: EDGAR is not a stock exchange, because no shares trade there, and it is a database where companies file reports with the SEC.

rw: A broker acts as an agent for customers, executing their orders for a commission, while a dealer trades from its own inventory as principal, which is the key distinction.

ww.A broker never charges fees, while a dea: Brokers do charge fees, often commissions, and dealers earn through spreads, so claiming a broker never charges fees is false and the roles differ differently.
ww.They are the same in every way, since bo: Brokers and dealers are not the same, because a dealer takes the other side of the trade using its own account, whereas a broker only arranges the trade.
ww.A broker owns the stock and a dealer doe: A broker does not own the stock it arranges trades for, and it is the dealer that holds inventory, so this option reverses the two roles.

rw: Best execution is the duty to seek the most favorable terms reasonably available for a customer's order, considering price, speed and likelihood of execution, so the customer is protected.

ww.A duty to avoid trading in any security: Avoiding any security the firm holds is not required, because firms may trade such securities, and best execution is about getting good terms for customers.
ww.A duty to charge the highest commission,: Charging the highest commission would harm customers, and best execution requires seeking favorable terms for them, so a duty to overcharge makes no sense.
ww.A duty to delay all orders until the mar: Delaying all orders until the market closes would hurt customers by missing prices and is not required, because best execution is about getting the best reasonable terms.

rw: Payment for order flow is compensation a broker receives from a market maker for routing customer orders to it, which raises conflict of interest concerns about best execution.

ww.A bonus that a fund pays to investors wh: A bonus for investors who stay invested is a loyalty or fee rebate and is not payment for order flow, which is paid to brokers by market makers.
ww.A tax that the government charges on eve: The government does not charge a tax on every trade for this, and payment for order flow is a payment to brokers from market makers, not a tax.
ww.A fee that customers pay to see live pri: A fee for seeing live prices is a market data fee, which customers sometimes pay, and it is not payment for order flow, which brokers receive from market makers.

rw: A wrap fee account charges one bundled fee that covers advice, trading and custody, so the client pays a single percentage of assets instead of separate commissions.

ww.An account only for bonds, which cannot: A wrap fee account is not limited to bonds, because it can hold a range of securities, and the name refers to how the fees are bundled.
ww.An account with no fees of any kind, as: A wrap fee account does charge a fee, since a single bundled fee covers services, so claiming no fees of any kind is false.
ww.An account that wraps gifts for the holi: Wrapping holiday gifts has nothing to do with banking, and the word wrap in a wrap fee means bundling several services into one fee.

rw: A fee-only adviser is paid only by clients, through fees, and not by commissions on products, which reduces conflicts of interest from product sales.

ww.An adviser who charges nothing and earns: A fee-only adviser does charge clients directly and does not live off a bank's profits, so describing the adviser as charging nothing is wrong.
ww.An adviser who works for free as a volun: A volunteer at a community center is not working as a fee-only adviser, since such advisers earn a living through client fees for their professional services.
ww.An adviser paid only by commissions on t: An adviser paid only by commissions on products sold is a commission-based adviser, which is the opposite of fee-only compensation.

rw: A commission-based adviser is paid mainly through commissions on the products sold to clients, which can create conflicts of interest between the adviser and the client.

ww.An adviser paid only by clients with no: An adviser paid only by clients with no commissions is fee-only, which is the opposite of commission-based, where pay comes from product sales.
ww.An adviser who is a volunteer and takes: A volunteer who takes no payment is not a commission-based adviser, because this type of adviser earns income from commissions on products sold.
ww.An adviser employed by the government to: A government employee counseling taxpayers is not a commission-based adviser, since public employees earn salaries and not commissions on investment products.

rw: A Wells notice is a letter from SEC staff saying it intends to recommend enforcement action, which gives the recipient a chance to respond before any formal action.

ww.A notice of a stock split sent to holder: A stock split notice informs holders of new share counts, which is routine corporate communication, and a Wells notice is an enforcement notice from the SEC staff.
ww.A notice of a bank holiday that tells cu: A bank holiday notice tells customers about branch closures, which has no relation to a Wells notice, a securities enforcement document.
ww.A notice about a new account that confir: A new account confirmation tells the client about a deposit and fees, whereas a Wells notice warns that enforcement action may be recommended.

rw: A cease-and-desist order is a regulatory order directing a person or firm to stop an unlawful practice, and it can be issued by agencies such as the SEC.

ww.An order to buy more shares at the next: An order to buy more shares at the next opening is a trade order and not a regulatory order, which is what a cease-and-desist order is.
ww.An order to open a new branch issued to: An order to open a new branch is a business decision and is not what a cease-and-desist order is, which is a regulatory command to stop conduct.
ww.An order to pay a dividend to all stockh: An order to pay a dividend would come from a board of directors, not a regulator, and it is not the same as a cease-and-desist order.

rw: Disgorgement requires wrongdoers to give up ill-gotten gains, such as profits from fraud or insider trading, so they cannot keep money obtained through illegal conduct.

ww.Paying a bonus to the staff of a firm th: Paying a bonus to staff who met goals is a reward and the opposite of disgorgement, which takes profits away from people who broke the rules.
ww.Splitting a stock into more shares at a: Splitting a stock into more shares at a lower price is a stock split, a corporate action, and it has nothing to do with surrendering profits.
ww.Reducing fees that a fund charges to its: Reducing the fees that a fund charges is a cost cut that benefits investors, which differs from disgorgement, where wrongdoers return profits obtained illegally.

rw: Controlling is one of the four classic management functions, along with planning, organizing and leading, and it involves monitoring performance and correcting deviations from the plan.

ww.Auditing: Auditing is a specialized accounting and review activity, but it is not one of the four classic management functions of planning, organizing, leading and controlling.
ww.Advertising: Advertising is a marketing activity, which is a business function and not one of the four management functions of planning, organizing, leading and controlling.
ww.Manufacturing: Manufacturing is an operations activity of making products, so it is a business function and not one of the four management functions, which are planning, organizing, leading and controlling.

rw: Planning is the management function of setting goals and deciding how to reach them, so it comes first and guides organizing, leading and controlling afterward.

ww.Controlling: Controlling means monitoring results and correcting deviations from the plan, which comes after goals are set, so it is not the function of setting goals.
ww.Organizing: Organizing means arranging people, tasks and resources to carry out the plan, which follows goal setting and is not the function of choosing goals.
ww.Leading: Leading means motivating and guiding people to reach goals, which is about people and direction, not about deciding the goals and how to reach them.

rw: Middle managers carry out top management's plans and supervise first-line managers, serving as the link that turns company strategy into day-to-day operations in departments and units.

ww.Sets the company's long-term goals and d: Setting long-term goals and direction is the job of top management, not middle managers, who work at a level below the top executives.
ww.Performs all of the entry-level tasks in: Performing entry-level tasks daily is the work of front-line employees, not middle managers, whose role is to coordinate and supervise rather than do all the basic tasks.
ww.Owns most of the company's shares and vo: Owning most of the shares and voting them at meetings is the role of major shareholders, which is not what a middle manager does as an employee.
